claims.text: Tailored thermal processing can control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
Controlled annealing followed by variation of the cooling rate can promote or suppress diffusion-mediated phase transformations.
The proposed initial state is a homogenized Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy with a high-temperature disordered structure.
Annealing at sufficiently high temperature homogenizes the alloy.
Rapid post-annealing cooling freezes in the disordered structure.
Slow post-annealing cooling permits diffusion and nucleation of ordered phases.
Cooling rate changes the diffusion kinetics governing nucleation and growth of ordered intermetallic phases.
B2 ordering is an example of an ordered transformation that may be governed by cooling-rate-dependent diffusion kinetics in this alloy system.
Cooling rate can determine whether a single-phase disordered structure is preserved.
Slow cooling gives atoms sufficient time to rearrange and form ordered phases.
Rapid quenching limits atomic mobility and retains the high-temperature disordered phase.
Rapid quenching will produce a predominantly disordered, single-phase Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA.
Slow cooling will produce a dual-phase microstructure containing ordered intermetallic features.
Formation of the proposed dual-phase microstructure may alter mechanical properties.
The as-cast or rapidly quenched alloy has a mostly disordered microstructure.
Cooling-rate control is effective only within a suitable cooling-rate window.
Excessively slow cooling may form unwanted coarse phases.
Extremely rapid cooling may stress or distort the material.
The thermal parameters required for a desired phase balance may depend on minor compositional variations or impurities.
If identically annealed samples subjected to rapid and slow cooling have no significant difference in ordered-phase formation, the proposed cooling-rate effect would be falsified.
